passages.t: Jehu's rebuke, and some good found
passages.happening: Jehoshaphat returns safely to Jerusalem (verse 1). Jehu son of Hanani the seer goes out to meet him: “Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD? Because of this, the wrath of the LORD is upon you” (verse 2). ‘However, some good is found in you, for you have removed the Asherah poles from the land and have set your heart on seeking God’ (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 18 ended with Jehoshaphat narrowly escaping death in Ahab's war. This short chapter shows how he answered that experience and a prophet's correction. Unlike his father Asa, who jailed the seer Hanani, Jehoshaphat accepts the rebuke of Hanani's son and turns it into reform.

Jehu son of Hanani belonged to a family of prophets. His father had rebuked Asa, and Jehu himself had pronounced judgment on Baasha of Israel; Chronicles later says he wrote an account of Jehoshaphat's reign. His word follows a pattern used elsewhere in Chronicles: rebuke, then a weighing of the good. In Hebrew covenant language, to love can mean to be loyal to or allied with, as in treaties.
passages.later: First Kings records Jehu's earlier word to Baasha: ‘Then the word of the LORD came to Jehu son of Hanani against Baasha’ (1 Kings 16:1).
passages.hard:
Jehu asks whether Jehoshaphat should love those who hate the LORD. Doesn't Jesus command love for enemies?

Jehu's rebuke concerns a particular political and military alliance. Jehoshaphat had joined his house to Ahab's by marriage and fought Ahab's war, lending his strength to a king who promoted the worship of Baal. In covenant language, to love can mean to be loyal to or ally with. The rebuke is about a partnership that supported the enemies of God and drew Judah into their idolatry, which the next chapters show happening through the marriage of Jehoram and Athaliah.

Jesus' command to love enemies calls for goodwill, prayer and kindness toward one's opponents. The two teachings address different things: one forbids yoking oneself to another's evil, the other forbids hatred and revenge. Christians have often heard in Paul's warning about being unequally yoked a New Testament parallel to Jehu's word.
passages.asks: Jehoshaphat heard a hard word and did not punish the messenger. Ask how you receive correction. And ask whether some alliance in your life is lending your strength to something you would not choose to serve.

passages.t: Judges for every city, and the fear of the LORD
passages.happening:
Jehoshaphat goes out again among the people ‘from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim and turned them back to the LORD, the God of their fathers’ (verse 4). He appoints judges in each fortified city of Judah (verse 5) and tells them, “Consider carefully what you do, for you are not judging for man, but for the LORD, who is with you when you render judgment” (verse 6). “And now, may the fear of the LORD be upon you. Be careful what you do, for with the LORD our God there is no injustice or partiality or bribery” (verse 7).

In Jerusalem he sets Levites, priests and family heads to judge for the LORD and settle disputes (verse 8), charging them, “You must serve faithfully and wholeheartedly in the fear of the LORD” (verse 9). Amariah the chief priest will be over them in matters of the LORD, and Zebadiah in matters of the king. ‘Act resolutely; may the LORD be with the upright’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The chapter's attention to justice fits the king's name, which means the LORD judges; the verb, shaphat, includes governing and setting things right. The reform appears only in Chronicles. Scholars debate how much reflects Jehoshaphat's own time and how much the institutions of the Chronicler's day; some find a royal organization of justice in the ninth century entirely plausible, others see later patterns in the details. The text presents it as Jehoshaphat's work.

Justice was ordinarily done by the elders of each town at the gate. Deuteronomy commanded judges in every town and a higher court at the central sanctuary for hard cases, and Jehoshaphat's arrangement follows that pattern. The highest court divided religious matters from royal ones. Bribery, shochad, and partiality were the great corruptions of ancient justice, as they are of modern justice. Jehoshaphat grounds the ban in the character of God: with the LORD there is no injustice, partiality or bribery, so those who judge for him must be the same. The fear of the LORD, yir'ah, for a judge means remembering whose court it finally is. Faithfully, emunah, is related to amen.
passages.later: The law said, ‘Do not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and twists the words of the righteous’ (Deuteronomy 16:19).
passages.asks: The judges were told that they were not judging for man but for the LORD. Ask where you make judgments that affect others, at work, at home or in a church, and whose court you think you sit in. And ask whether anything has quietly bought your favor.
